situation:
You are the financial analyst for HALVORSEN PHARMACEUTICAL SUPPLY, a family-owned distributor that buys prescription medicines from manufacturers in Europe and delivers them to hospitals and clinics across a three-state region. The president (judge) is the third generation of the family to run the business and has asked you to recommend how the company will protect next year's profit.

Nearly every case HALVORSEN PHARMACEUTICAL SUPPLY buys is priced in euros and paid for ninety days after it ships. When the euro rises against the dollar between the order and the payment, the cost of goods rises with it, and the company absorbs the difference because its customer prices are set a year at a time. That single exposure has moved the company's margin more than anything else on the books.

The company's bank has offered forward contracts the company can buy to fix the euro cost for a full year. The contracts carry a fee that is paid whether or not the rate moves, and that fee comes out of the same margin the twelve rural clinic accounts earn, which is the thinnest margin on the customer list. If the euro falls instead of rising, the company pays above the market rate for the whole year.

The other path is on the shipping floor. The warehouse is already packing at its limit and cannot add orders without a second shift, and the signed one-year agreement with the hospital chain commits the company to a larger monthly volume the chain wants delivered. Freeing that space means the company would stop serving the twelve rural clinics and give their warehouse space to the hospital chain, ending a relationship the family built over fifteen years; those clinics would be left without another distributor in the region.

The president (judge) wants you to analyze the transactions behind the swing, identify which factors are actually moving profit, and recommend one of the two paths. The president (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the president (judge) of HALVORSEN PHARMACEUTICAL SUPPLY. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You are the third generation of your family to run this distributor, and next year's profit is the first one you will report on your own. You want the financial analyst to tell you which of the two paths to take — the bank's forward contracts, or clearing warehouse space by dropping the twelve rural clinic accounts — and you want to hear how the decision would be explained to the people it lands on hardest.

During the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: Who does this decision land hardest on?
How would you tell them, and what would you say?
